title: Unlimited OCR: Constant KV Cache for Long Documents
hook: LLM-based OCR slows down as documents get longer because the KV cache keeps growing. Unlimited OCR holds the cache constant, transcribing dozens of pages in one pass.
key_points: End-to-end OCR with an LLM decoder (e.g., DeepSeek OCR) slows as output grows — the KV cache keeps expanding.
Unlimited OCR replaces the decoder's attention with Reference Sliding Window Attention (R-SWA), keeping the KV cache constant throughout decoding.
Paired with DeepSeek OCR's high-compression encoder, it transcribes dozens of pages in a single forward pass within a 32K length.
R-SWA is general-purpose parsing attention — usable beyond OCR for tasks like ASR and translation.
Released open: a 3.3B multilingual model (MIT) on GitHub and ModelScope, with base and 'gundam' image modes.
content_html: End-to-end OCR models with LLM decoders — DeepSeek OCR being the headline example — put OCR back in the spotlight by letting the decoder lean on a language model's priors. But there's a catch: as the output sequence grows, the accumulated KV cache drives up memory and progressively slows generation. Humans don't slow down copying a long document; these models do. Yin, Liu, Jia and colleagues at Baidu address that with Unlimited OCR.
extra_html:
How it works

Taking DeepSeek OCR as the baseline, Unlimited OCR replaces all attention layers in the decoder with Reference Sliding Window Attention (R-SWA), which reduces attention cost and — critically — keeps the KV cache constant throughout the entire decoding process. Combined with DeepSeek OCR's high-compression encoder, that constant-cache design lets the model transcribe dozens of pages of documents in a single forward pass under a standard 32K maximum length.

Why it matters

R-SWA isn't OCR-specific: the authors frame it as a general-purpose parsing attention mechanism applicable to tasks like ASR and translation, wherever a model emits long sequences. The work is released openly — a 3.3B multilingual model under an MIT license on GitHub and ModelScope, with base and "gundam" image modes for different layouts — making the constant-KV trick easy to study.

related.title: The KV Cache & Continuous Batching
related.hook: Generating one token reuses every prior key and value - that growing cache is why LLM inference is memory-bound, and continuous batching is how servers fight back.

related.title: Multi-Query Attention: Faster Decoding
related.hook: Share one key/value head across all query heads - the KV cache shrinks by a factor of H and decoding gets dramatically faster with barely any quality cost.

related.title: PagedAttention / vLLM: Efficient LLM Serving
related.hook: LLM serving wastes huge amounts of GPU memory on the attention cache. PagedAttention borrows an OS trick — paging — to recover it and serve many more requests at once.

flashcards.prompt: Why does LLM-decoder OCR slow down on long documents, and how does Unlimited OCR fix it?
flashcards.back_html: The KV cache grows with output length, raising memory and slowing generation; Reference Sliding Window Attention (R-SWA) keeps the KV cache constant throughout decoding.

flashcards.prompt: What does R-SWA's constant KV cache buy for OCR?

choices.text: It can transcribe dozens of pages in one forward pass without speed and memory degrading as output grows
It raises character accuracy by using a much larger cache
It removes the need for a vision encoder

flashcards.explanation_html: A constant-size cache means cost doesn't balloon with output length, so very long transcriptions stay efficient in a single pass under a 32K limit.

flashcards.prompt: Beyond OCR, where else can R-SWA apply?
flashcards.back_html: It's a general-purpose parsing attention mechanism, applicable to other long-output sequence tasks such as ASR (speech recognition) and translation.
